h1: Filming your brewing process for social media without boring viewers
title: Filming Your Brewing Process for Social | Craft Beer School
desc: How to film brew day for Instagram and YouTube so viewers keep watching: what to shoot, how to keep it short, safety on camera and staying within the rules.
teaser: Mashing in is magic to a brewer and a static shot of porridge to everyone else. Here is how to film it so it is neither.
standfirst: Brewing looks fascinating up close: steam, foam, hops, shining steel. Most brewery videos still lose viewers in seconds. Here is how to film the process so people watch to the end.
sections:
A brewer filming their own brew day tends to show what matters to them: the mash temperature, the gravity reading, the slow transfer. To a viewer scrolling Instagram, that looks like a man staring at a tank. The process is interesting, but only when it is shown with movement, close-ups and a reason to keep watching.

The aim is not to teach brewing in sixty seconds. It is to show viewers that real people make your beer with care and to make them want to taste it.

• Grain pouring into the mill or mash tun, close and slow.
  • Steam rising off the kettle at the start of the boil.
  • Hop additions: green pellets or cones hitting boiling wort.
  • The hot break foaming up in the kettle.
  • Hands at work: checking a sample, tasting, adjusting a valve.
  • The pour: the finished beer into a clean glass, with a good head.

Each of these is a few seconds of real movement. Strung together, they tell the story of a beer from grain to glass in under a minute. Our guide to how beer is made is a useful shot list if you want to follow the full process.

For a short vertical video, the first two seconds decide whether people keep watching. Open with the most striking shot, not the brewery sign. Then show the steps in order, with quick cuts. End on the finished beer and a simple call, such as when it goes on tap.

Add captions. Many people watch with the sound off. Captions also help viewers who do not know brewing words. A line like "Hops in, 60 minutes to go" gives just enough context.

Longer videos on YouTube can go deeper, such as a full brew day or a brewer explaining a recipe. Even there, cut out the waiting. Nobody needs ninety minutes of a mash rest.

People are what keep viewers watching longer pieces. Let the brewer explain one decision on camera, such as why a hop goes in late or why the lager sits cold for weeks. A single clear reason, said by the person who made it, is more watchable than any amount of stainless steel.

A modern phone is enough. What matters more is light and steadiness. Brewhouses are often dim with harsh overhead lights. Shoot near windows when you can, or use a small LED light. A cheap phone stand or gimbal stops the shaky look. For talking to camera, a clip-on microphone makes a huge difference against the noise of pumps and fans.

Steam fogs lenses fast, so wipe the lens between shots. Wort and cleaning chemicals do not mix well with phones, so use a case.

A brewhouse has real hazards: boiling wort, caustic cleaning chemicals, CO2 and pressurised tanks. Anything you film should show safe practice, with proper gloves, eye protection, closed shoes and no one leaning into a kettle for a shot. Viewers include other brewers and inspectors. A careless video can do more harm than none. Never film inside a fermenter or confined space, which can hold dangerous levels of CO2.

Alcohol advertising is restricted in India. Platforms have their own policies on alcohol content. Showing how beer is made is generally safer than promoting drinking. Avoid scenes of heavy drinking, anything aimed at younger audiences and claims about effects. Use age restrictions where the platform allows them. Our guide to alcohol advertising rules in India explains the background. When in doubt, ask an adviser.

The breweries with good video channels film a little every brew day rather than planning big productions. Keep a phone stand by the brewhouse. Grab a few clips at each key step. Over a month, you will have enough for several short videos and a longer piece.

Then watch which videos people finish and share. That tells you what your audience finds interesting, which may not be what you expected. Planning that content around your release calendar and audience is what turns a few clips into a channel.
faqs: What phone or camera do I need to film brewing?
A recent phone is enough. Good light, a stand to keep it steady and a clip-on microphone matter more than the camera.
How long should a brewing video for Instagram be?
For short vertical videos, under a minute works well. Open with your strongest shot and cut out any waiting.
Is it legal to post brewing videos in India?
Showing the process is generally treated differently from promoting drinking, but alcohol advertising rules and platform policies apply. Avoid drinking scenes and take advice if unsure.
